title: Concept Drills — Reflection at Curved Mirror (Class 11 Physics)
subject: physics

questions.question: How can a mirror — a surface — produce a REAL image that can be caught on a screen?
questions.solution: A concave mirror CONVERGES reflected rays: rays from a point outside the focus actually intersect after reflection, forming a real image where light physically concentrates (hot at that spot, visible on a screen). Plane and convex mirrors only diverge rays — their images are the intersections of backward EXTENSIONS, hence virtual.

questions.question: Why is a spherical mirror's focal length half its radius of curvature? Use the geometry of a ray parallel to the axis.
questions.solution: A ray parallel to the axis strikes at angle θ and reflects at θ; the triangle formed with the centre of curvature C is isosceles, so the point where the reflected ray crosses the axis (F) sits midway between pole and C — f = R/2 (exact only for small apertures, where sinθ ≈ θ).

questions.question: Why does a convex mirror give a virtual, erect, diminished image for EVERY object position, and why are they used as vehicle mirrors?
questions.solution: A convex mirror diverges reflected rays — they only appear to come from a point BEHIND the mirror, so the image is always virtual and erect; the divergence makes the image smaller than the object. Smallness buys FIELD OF VIEW: a wide scene compresses into the mirror, which is exactly what a driver needs — at the cost of distance misjudgement ('objects are closer than they appear').

questions.question: An object 30 cm from a concave mirror (f = 10 cm): set up 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with signs and interpret the result.
questions.solution: u = −30 cm (object in front), f = −10 cm (concave). 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/10 + 1/30 = −2/30 → v = −15 cm. Negative v: image on the same side as the object — real, inverted, magnified m = −v/u = −0.5 (diminished since object is beyond C). Signs carry the geometry; magnitudes alone mislead.

questions.question: Why is the same concave mirror useful both as a searchlight reflector and as a dentist's mirror?
questions.solution: Reversibility of light: a source at the focus sends out parallel rays (searchlight) — and rays from a close object converge to a magnified virtual image when the object is inside f (dentist's mirror). One geometry, two uses depending on where the light source/object sits relative to F.

questions.concept: Why a convex mirror always gives a small virtual image
questions.question: A convex mirror can only form a diminished, virtual image whatever the object distance. Why can it never form a real image?
questions.solution: A convex mirror's centre of curvature and focus both lie BEHIND the mirror, so reflected rays always diverge. Because they diverge, they cannot meet on the reflecting side; they only appear to meet behind the mirror when extended backward. Real images require converging rays. Convex mirrors are therefore used as wide-angle rear-view and security mirrors.

questions.question: Two concave-mirror images have magnifications −2 and +2. What does each tell you about the image?
questions.solution: The sign encodes ORIENTATION, not size: both are twice the object's size. m negative means inverted (real image, formed by actual converging rays in front of the mirror); m positive means erect (virtual image, behind the mirror, from extended rays). Magnitude alone is incomplete information — always read the sign, using the sign convention consistently.

questions.concept: Why a dentist uses a concave mirror
questions.question: A dentist holds the mirror close to a tooth to see it magnified. Why must it be close, and why concave?
questions.solution: Placing the object between the pole and the focus of a concave mirror produces a virtual, erect, MAGNIFIED image. If it were farther away the image would invert and shrink (past C) or become real. Both the concave shape and the short object distance are required — the magnification comes from being inside the focal length.
